_description: THE source of every TrainConfig value. The dataclass declares the schema - field names, types, and what each knob does - and holds no values: each field's default is read from here. Editing this file changes what `python -m gym_continuousDoubleAuction.train.train` does, with no flag needed. Every field must be present; a missing key raises when a TrainConfig is built. Groups are flattened one level, keys starting with _ are documentation, unknown keys raise. Derived properties (train_batch_size, checkpoint_dir) are computed in code and are not listed.
_note: Precedence is this file -> `--config <other file>` -> explicit CLI flags. The `environment` group is forwarded to the env by TrainConfig.env_config, which renames exactly one key: num_agents here becomes num_of_agents in the env config dict. num_trained_agents is NOT forwarded - it configures the policy/module wiring, not the env. A bare env built without these keys falls back to config/env_defaults.json, whose standalone values deliberately differ from the training values here. The ppo and league_self_play groups are also read directly by model_handler.default_model_config and SelfPlayCallback when those are called without arguments.

environment._note_mark_price_source: See env_defaults.json. 'mid' marks every account at the L1 midpoint (falling back to a one-sided quote, then to the last tape print); 'last' reproduces the previous last-print-only behaviour. Marking off the last print is what made self-matching profitable - finding S2-5.
environment._note_episode_length: See env_defaults.json. In 'random' mode train_batch_size is the mean horizon times num_episodes_per_iter.
environment._note_book_mode: See env_defaults.json. 'grid' (fixed tick-offset window shared by observation and action, S3-15) or 'levels' (the k_rows best occupied prices per side). Changing it is a layout change: a checkpoint records its mode and is refused by a run in the other.
environment._note_action_mask: See env_defaults.json. false emits an all-ones mask, the unmasked baseline for train.compare.
environment._note_matching: See env_defaults.json. matching_rule 'fifo' or 'pro_rata'; step_clearing 'sequential' or 'batch'. Both change the game the agents play, so a checkpoint trained under one regime is a different policy from one trained under another; compare them with train.compare --set.
environment._note_liquidation: See env_defaults.json. 'market_adl' closes out a trader below maintenance_margin through the book, then ADL for the remainder; 'gradual_adl' is the same spread over up to liquidation_horizon steps; 'off' is the earlier behaviour, where a bankrupt trader keeps its position to the end of the episode. Both change the game, so compare them with train.compare --set liquidation=off.
environment._note_position_scale: position_scale divides net_position before the tanh in the private observation block. Deliberately not limit_max_size, which is what it used to be: that is a sizing parameter - it scales the mean of the Gaussian _set_size draws from and bounds nothing - while inventory accumulates over many fills. Measured over 7,200 agent-steps of random play at default config, |net_position| has a median of 372, a p90 of 1,195, a p95 of 1,485 and a maximum of 1,831, so limit_max_size of 1,000 put 13.2% of agent-steps into tanh saturation. 1500 is that p95, which keeps the feature in its responsive range across the observed distribution (finding S2-2).
environment._note_reward_coefficients: See config/env_defaults.json for how these are scaled and why loss_multiplier is 1.0. Both files must agree; test_config_sources pins the fallback behaviour.
environment._note_dead_action_penalty: dead_action_penalty multiplies num_unmatched_step - modify/cancel actions this step that named no resting order (doc/15 S3-24 phase 3). Zero by default, deliberately: any positive value makes sum(reward) < 0 across agents, which is the negative-sum bias finding S1-3 removed, so turning it on is a measured decision, not a default. The miss is already visible to the policy through the unmatched_last_step observation field, which costs nothing.

rollouts._note: sample_timeout_s is how long the driver waits for a remote env runner to return its share of train_batch_size (= max_step * num_episodes_per_iter) before giving up on it. RLlib's default is 60s, which this environment cannot meet: the order book is pure Python at roughly 60 env steps/s per runner, so 16,384 steps across 2 runners needs ~2 minutes. A timed-out iteration is not a slow iteration - the partial rollouts are discarded, the learner is handed nothing, and the run does zero gradient work while still logging iterations and writing checkpoints. Size this above the time one iteration's sampling actually takes, or shrink the batch by lowering max_step / num_episodes_per_iter. It is ignored when num_env_runners is 0, since the driver then samples in-process.

optimizer._note: Adam settings RLlib would otherwise leave at torch's defaults. Both continual-backprop papers run every algorithm except the standard-PPO baseline with beta_1 = beta_2 = 0.99, on the grounds that the usual (0.9, 0.999) mismatch is itself a cause of plasticity loss: the squared-gradient estimate in the denominator updates far more slowly than the gradient estimate in the numerator, so a single large gradient produces one very large, destabilising update. The Nature paper also applies continual backprop together with L2 (weight decay 1e-4) in every reinforcement-learning experiment, and reports that CBP alone is sensitive to the replacement rate while the pair is not. The defaults below are torch's, so a run that changes neither gets exactly the optimiser RLlib has always built, and every existing checkpoint is unaffected. Deliberately a separate group from continual_backprop: enabling CBP and retuning Adam at the same time would measure the two together, and the papers treat them as independent interventions that happen to be used together.

continual_backprop._note: Continual Backprop (Dohare, Hernandez-Garcia, Lan, Rahman, Mahmood & Sutton, Nature 2024; Dohare, Sutton & Mahmood, arXiv 2108.06325). Backprop plus a generate-and-test process that continually reinitialises the lowest-utility hidden units: incoming weights resampled from the layer's initial distribution, outgoing weights set to zero so the fresh unit reaches the output not at all. It is an update rule, not an architecture, so it composes over whichever Learner the encoder selected rather than occupying the encoder registry's single learner slot - see doc/25 section 2.5. Off by default, and when off the resolved learner class is identical to the one a run would have had before this group existed.
continual_backprop._note_restore: cbp_enabled and cbp_metrics_only are UNRESTORABLE_CONFIG_KEYS: changing either in the same pass as is_restore is a hard error, and so is changing any of the tuning knobs below while continual backprop is running on either side (UNRESTORABLE_WHEN_ACTIVE_KEYS - a knob edited while the mechanism is off in both the checkpoint and the config is allowed, because it describes something that was not going to happen either way). Not for the reason encoder_spec is - no tensor shape depends on these, and the weights would restore perfectly well - but because they are consumed when the Learner class is chosen and the optimiser is built, both of which happen before a restore, after which Algorithm.from_checkpoint rebuilds from the checkpoint's own config and discards them. Turning continual backprop on alongside a resume therefore did nothing at all, and looked identical to a run that honoured it. Changing any of these means a fresh run, not a resume. The per-unit utility and ages ARE checkpoint state and are restored with the learner; a checkpoint written before this group existed restores cleanly and starts every unit at age 0.
continual_backprop._note_cadence: cbp_replacement_rate and cbp_maturity_threshold are both counted in OPTIMISER STEPS - not environment steps, and not training iterations. This repo takes 4 Adam steps per iteration at its defaults (num_epochs 4 over one full batch, minibatch_size null) against the 320 of the papers' Continual PPO (10 epochs x 32 minibatches), so the papers' own PPO values cannot be transplanted: their maturity threshold of 1e4 would be 2,500 iterations here, against a default run of 16, and no unit would ever become mature. cbp_maturity_threshold is therefore the arXiv CBP default of 100 rather than the Nature PPO value. Watch cbp_replacements and cbp_mature_unit_frac: a continual backprop that never fires looks exactly like one that is working, and at low replacement rates over a short run not firing is the expected outcome.
continual_backprop._note_metrics_only: cbp_metrics_only computes the utility and logs the three correlates of loss of plasticity - dead units, weight magnitude, effective rank - without replacing anything, so it cannot change a run's trajectory. That is the measurement doc/25 recommends taking before switching the mechanism on, and it has now been taken: at ~20,000 optimiser steps on the scaled-down default config, at one seed, no loss of plasticity is detectable (doc/25 section 3.3, doc/16 section 16.16). Dead and saturated units sat at exactly zero throughout, and the network's rank on a FIXED corpus moved by +2.5% to -1.9% while cbp_batch_effective_rank fell 24.6% - the fall being the policy narrowing its own inputs, not the network losing capacity. That null does not carry to the 1e6-1e8 steps this project needs, which is the run still to do; read train/probe/rank.py across checkpoints rather than the batch metric when doing it.
continual_backprop._note_scope: cbp_scope selects which units are replaceable. 'feedforward' means the hidden units of a two-Linear feed-forward block, plus the trunk's final hidden layer whose outgoing weights live in the pi/vf head rather than the encoder. Attention projections and embeddings are excluded: a unit there has no single well-defined outgoing weight matrix, and zeroing the outgoing weights is the whole reason a replacement does not disturb the function. Layers no optimiser trains are also skipped, which is what keeps it off the jepa encoder's EMA target trunk.
continual_backprop._note_utility: cbp_utility selects the measure ranked against. 'contribution' is Nature equation 1, |h| * sum|w_out|. 'mean_corrected' subtracts the running mean activation, because gradient descent transfers the mean part of a removed unit's contribution to the consumer's bias anyway. 'overall' additionally divides by sum|w_in|, the adaptation utility: under Adam a unit with small incoming weights can change its function faster, so it is worth more than its contribution alone suggests. arXiv Appendix C ablates all three and finds 'overall' best, including on the reinforcement-learning task, which is why it is the default here.
continual_backprop._note_fire_on: cbp_fire_on selects when generate-and-test runs. 'adam_step' is after every optimiser step, which is what arXiv Algorithm 3 (Continual PPO) specifies. 'iteration' runs it once per training iteration instead, which cannot move the network underneath a log-prob recorded before it and so leaves PPO's exp(logp_new - logp_old) ratio undisturbed between minibatches. The papers use the per-step placement over 100M steps, so it is the default, but the conservative one is kept available.

encoder._note: Selects the network the *trainable* PPO modules encode observations with. The frozen RandomRLModule baselines have no network and ignore this entirely. `mlp` is the default and is a pass-through: it resolves to the stock RLlib DefaultModelConfig built from the `ppo` group's fcnet_hiddens / fcnet_activation / vf_share_layers, touching none of the custom encoder machinery, so a default run and every checkpoint written by one are unaffected by this group existing. Any other value routes the trainable modules through CDACatalog and a custom encoder. An unregistered name raises at config-build time, naming the ones that are registered.
encoder._note_structural: encoder_type and everything in encoder_specs are STRUCTURAL_CONFIG_KEYS: the restored weights depend on them, so changing one in the same pass as is_restore is a hard error rather than a silent no-op. Comparing architectures means separate runs, not a resume.
encoder._note_specs: Per-architecture hyperparameters, keyed by encoder_type. `mlp` has no block: its shape comes from the `ppo` group, which is where it has always lived and where STRUCTURAL_CONFIG_KEYS already guards it. A block is added here alongside each new encoder, so an entry existing is the signal that its encoder is implemented.
encoder._note_common_keys: Two further keys are accepted in EVERY spec block and handled centrally: `lr` and `vf_share_layers`. Both defaults in the `ppo` group were chosen for the 2x256 tanh MLP - holding an attention stack to that learning rate measures the learning rate rather than the architecture, and vf_share_layers false doubles a transformer where it barely costs an MLP anything. Omit them to inherit the `ppo` group; set either to override it for that encoder only. They are not listed in the blocks below because absent means inherit, and a null would be indistinguishable from a value nobody chose.
encoder._note_pretrained: pretrained_encoder_path points at a directory written by `python -m gym_continuousDoubleAuction.train.pretrain`, whose weights the trainable modules start from instead of a fresh initialisation. null means no pretraining. The checkpoint carries an encoder fingerprint that is checked against encoder_type and encoder_specs when the module spec is built, so pointing at a checkpoint for a different architecture is a hard error there rather than a shape failure inside RLlib. It is NOT a structural key: it changes where the weights start, not their shape, so resuming a run that used one is fine - the restored checkpoint already contains whatever pretraining contributed. `mlp` cannot use one, having no self-supervised objective that could have produced the weights.

transformer._note: tokenization decides what a token is: 'time' = one per snapshot (n_hist of them - too few to attend over at n_hist 4, kept for ablation), 'level' = one per book level from the newest snapshot, 'both' = one per (snapshot, level) cell. Under 'level' and 'both' a token is that level's [bid_price, bid_size, ask_price, ask_size] and the market-level scalars ride on an extra global token per snapshot, so the sequence is n_hist * (k_rows + 1) long, not n_hist * k_rows.
transformer._note_dropout: Leave at 0 for PPO. The ratio exp(logp_new - logp_old) compares a log-prob recorded during rollout with one recomputed on the learner; dropout is active for the second and not the first, so a non-zero value injects mask noise directly into the policy-gradient ratio. The knob exists because it is standard on this component, not because it is advisable here.
transformer._note_cost: vf_share_layers in the ppo group is false, which builds two independent trunks - so a transformer here costs twice these numbers. That default is deliberate (a shared value trunk destabilises against non-stationary league opponents), so it is a real trade-off rather than a free saving.

lstm._note: The structured LSTM, not RLlib's use_lstm shortcut. tokenization / d_model / pool / num_heads configure the per-step tokenizer, which embeds one observation's book grid; hidden_dim / num_layers configure the LSTM that then recurs over the ROLLOUT axis on top of those embeddings. Two different time axes: the tokenizer collapses n_hist, which is a window inside one observation, while the LSTM's memory runs across env steps.
lstm._note_n_hist: Those two axes overlap. With n_hist 4 the LSTM re-reads the last four snapshots at every step, so its memory is partly redundant with the observation. Setting n_hist to 1 for a recurrent run removes that, at the cost of invalidating checkpoints - n_hist is structural.
lstm._note_max_seq_len: Applied to the top-level model config, not to the encoder: RLlib's connectors read it to cut a batch into training sequences before any encoder is called. It is declared in this block because it belongs to this encoder conceptually, and build_trainable_module_spec lifts it across.

moe_transformer._note: The transformer above with each block's dense feed-forward replaced by a top-k gated mixture of experts. Every transformer key means the same thing here, except that ff_dim is now each EXPERT's width - so the feed-forward parameter count is roughly num_experts times what the same ff_dim buys in `transformer`, while the per-token compute is top_k times it.
moe_transformer._note_aux: aux_loss_coeff weights the Switch-Transformer load-balancing term, which is the only thing pushing the gate to use more than one expert - nothing in the policy gradient rewards it for doing so, and collapsing onto a single expert is a perfectly good local optimum that yields a dense feed-forward you paid num_experts times over for. Read by CDAPPOTorchLearner, not by the encoder.
moe_transformer._note_aux_scale: The term is AVERAGED over MoE blocks, not summed, so this coefficient means the same thing whatever the stack looks like. Summed - which is what Switch Transformer does - it would scale with num_layers and double when vf_share_layers is false, because the critic's blocks route separately and count too: a coefficient tuned at num_layers 2 would apply twice the pressure at 4, silently, and comparing two MoE configs of different depths would confound depth with how hard the gate was being pushed. Averaged, the floor is top_k (2 at these settings) at perfectly uniform routing, so an untrained gate reads just above 2.
moe_transformer._note_expect_collapse: Set expectations. This env's observation is 216 floats (4 stacked 46-float snapshots plus a 32-float private block) and the league is small, so MoE's premise - capacity you cannot afford densely - may not apply. Watch moe_max_expert_share and moe_min_expert_share in the learner metrics. NOTE THE NORMALISATION: expert_fractions is built by scattering top_k ones per token, so it sums to top_k, not to 1 - uniform routing gives top_k/num_experts per expert (0.5 at the shipped top_k 2, num_experts 4), NOT 1/num_experts. Both notes here said 1/num_experts, which would read a perfectly healthy mixture as collapsed, and a collapsed one is indistinguishable from a healthy one by loss or throughput alone.

jepa._note: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. The transformer keys mean what they do in that block; the rest configure the self-supervised objective. Predicts MASKED TOKENS' LATENTS from the visible ones, scored against an EMA copy of the encoder - nothing reconstructs the input, which matters here because a reconstruction loss would be dominated by sqrt(volume) jitter (measured channel sigmas [1.27, 8.17, 0.046, 9.52]).
jepa._note_policy_latent: The POLICY latent is always computed from the UNMASKED observation - the agent acts on everything it was given. Masking exists only for the auxiliary loss, and runs in train mode only, so a training step costs two trunk passes plus the target's while inference costs exactly one, the same as `transformer`.
jepa._note_mask_axis: What a mask hides. 'level' hides a contiguous depth band in every snapshot (what depth is consistent with this touch?); 'time' hides whole snapshots (where is the book heading?); 'random' uses no structure and is the ablation baseline. Under 'level' tokenisation there is only one snapshot, so all three degenerate to random.
jepa._note_collapse: WATCH jepa_latent_std IN THE LEARNER METRICS. A collapsed JEPA drives its prediction loss to ZERO, which reads as success - loss and throughput look identical to a working one. latent_std goes to 0 exactly when every observation maps to the same latent and should sit near 1.0. variance_coeff weights a VICReg-style hinge that pushes back once it starts falling. Both the metric and the hinge are computed on the ONLINE side (the predictor's output), not on the EMA target: read off the target they carried no gradient at all and the term was a constant added to the loss - finding S2-9; jepa_offdiag_cov catches dimensional collapse, where variance holds up but the dimensions become redundant.
jepa._note_ema_decay: How slowly the target encoder follows the online one. The asymmetry - a frozen, lagging target the predictor has to chase - is the primary anti-collapse mechanism; a constant encoder cannot satisfy a moving target. Higher is slower and more stable; too high and the target carries no signal.
jepa._note_world_model: world_model turns on the ACTION-CONDITIONED term: predict the next observation's latent from this one's plus the action taken, z_hat_t+1 = P(z_t, a_t), scored against the EMA target encoder's view of o_t+1. What it learns is the latent market impact of an order - how the book responds to a market order versus a passive quote versus a cancel - which is a microstructure quantity this env generates endogenously. Off by default because it needs Columns.NEXT_OBS in the train batch, which PPO does not add; train.py attaches RLlib's learner connector for it ONLY when this is on, so no other architecture pays for a column it never reads. Honest bound: z_t+1 depends on every agent's action and this conditions on one of them, so the predictor fits a conditional expectation over the opponents. The loss therefore has a non-zero floor which is NOT underfitting - it is an opponent model, and tuning it away would mean overfitting to noise.

league_self_play._note: nav_tolerance is the absolute cash tolerance for the episode-end NAV conservation check. The ledger is Decimal end to end and the check now parses info['NAV'] back with Decimal rather than float, and the ledger carries each position's basis as the exact Decimal sum of trade values (not a rounded VWAP quotient - that lost the last digit until doc/15 S3-23 was fixed on 2026-09-18), so conservation is exact by construction and the expected error is 0, not merely small. test_orderbook_properties asserts it with ==. The tolerance is therefore headroom for a change that legitimately removes cash from the system, such as fees - it is not absorbing arithmetic noise. Widen it for such a change; it can be set to 0 for a run that wants the invariant enforced exactly. strict_nav_check true stops the run on a violation, because a broken conservation invariant means the ledger is corrupt and everything trained after it is meaningless; false downgrades it to an ERROR log plus the nav_conservation_error metric, for a run that would rather keep going and be inspected afterwards. The stop is decided on the driver at the end of the iteration, not raised inside the episode hook: that hook runs on the env runner, where RLlib's fault tolerance swallows the exception and restarts the worker instead of ending the run.
league_self_play._note_episode_record: episode_data_dir is the root of the per-step episode record, written as Parquet - one row per (episode, step, agent), carrying the whole info dict. null switches it off entirely, including the in-memory accumulation behind it. It is resolved to an absolute path with run_id appended before it reaches the callback, because the callback is pickled into every env runner and a relative path would be resolved against whatever working directory that worker inherited. episode_sample_every records one episode in N, chosen by a hash of the episode id so every runner samples the same subset without coordinating; the record is ~34MB per 4096-step episode, so this is what makes the default affordable. episode_max_bytes caps what each writer keeps, deleting its own oldest files first - per writer rather than per directory, because deleting another worker's files is a cross-process race for no benefit, so a run with N runners keeps up to N times this. episode_rows_per_file is the write batch: at num_agents rows per env step, a file is episode_rows_per_file / num_agents steps.

run._note: log_level is Ray's, passed to PPOConfig.debugging; cda_log_level is this package's own, applied by logging_setup and exported as $CDA_LOG_LEVEL so Ray's worker processes pick it up. They are separate because Ray at INFO is noise while this package at INFO is the per-episode NAV table and the per-iteration league statistics - the output a run is meant to produce. Set cda_log_level to DEBUG for the per-step render and account tables, WARNING for a quiet run. ray_log_encoding is handed to ray.LoggingConfig, which is the only lever that reaches a worker's Ray-side output - the env-runner restart notices and the traceback RLlib swallows when a runner dies are emitted by Ray's own loggers in processes this package never configures. TEXT keeps them human-readable with job and worker ids attached; JSON makes them machine-parseable; an empty string leaves Ray's logging entirely alone. Setting it also turns off propagation from this package's logger to the root one, since ray.LoggingConfig configures root and both handlers would otherwise print every line twice.
run._note_run: num_iters is a target, not an amount: a restored run trains up to iteration num_iters, so a 16-iteration run that resumes at 9 does 7 more. Set num_iters_is_delta true for the old behaviour, where num_iters is how many iterations to run from wherever the restore landed. restore_path pins which checkpoint to resume from; null takes the newest under log_base_dir/chkpt, which is what a disconnect wants. It requires is_restore, and is deliberately recorded here rather than passed at the call site, so which checkpoint a run continued from is written down beside the run.
run._note_run_id: Names the per-run directory under log_base_dir that holds progress.jsonl and the run logs. null generates one from the local date, time and four random hex digits, so two runs never write into each other's files - a shared run.log is the cross-process RotatingFileHandler race the per-worker files exist to avoid, and a shared progress.jsonl can interleave two drivers' writes inside a single JSON line. Set it to a fixed string to resume into an existing run directory and extend its progress.jsonl, which is what a disconnected run that is being restored wants. The checkpoint tree deliberately stays at log_base_dir/chkpt, outside the run directory: restore looks for the newest iter_* across runs, so scoping it per run would make every resumed run start from nothing.
